title:
Plastic Flows and
Footprints in Norway’s Sea-Based
Aquaculture Sector: A Material Flow Perspective

affiliation.name: Norwegian University of Science and Technology , , 106, Gamle Fysikk, Sem Sælands vei 5 , ,
Norwegian University of Science and Technology , , Sem Sælands vei 7 , ,
Norwegian University of Science and Technology , , Sem Sælands vei 7 , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Marine plastic pollution is an increasing environmental concern, yet aquaculture’s contribution remains poorly quantified despite its rapid expansion and reliance on plastic infrastructure. Limited data on plastic stocks, flows, losses, and end-of-life (EOL) management constrain effective mitigation and circularity strategies. This study presents a system-wide assessment of plastic use and management in Norway’s sea-based Atlantic salmon aquaculture industry. A static Material Flow Analysis (MFA), informed by data from equipment manufacturers, suppliers, operators, and waste-management stakeholders, quantifies plastic stocks and flows across equipment deployment, use, repair, replacement, environmental losses, and end-of-life treatment. The results indicate annual marine plastic losses of approximately 2737 t, corresponding to 1.2–1.7 kg per tonne of salmon produced. Feed pipes, walkway components, and consumable ropes dominate leakage. Approximately 37,400 t of end-of-life plastics are collected annually, with 42% directed to incineration with energy recovery, 22% landfilled, and limited recovery through recycling. These findings highlight substantial opportunities to strengthen collection, recycling, and resource recovery. This first comprehensive national-scale assessment establishes a quantitative baseline for monitoring and policy development. It demonstrates MFA’s utility for identifying leakage hotspots and supporting Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) and circular economy strategies to reduce plastic pollution from aquaculture.</jats:p>

title:
Products of Indoor
Ozone Chemistry Are Associated
with Office Workers’ Negative Emotion
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Numerous chemicals, emitted from humans, building materials, and cleaning agents, are present at high concentrations in modern energy-saving buildings with low air change rates (ACRs). Outdoor ozone entering indoors oxidizes these chemicals on surfaces and in the air to form more toxic compounds, collectively termed ozone reaction products (ORPs). In this study, 141 participants working in two open-plan offices within a commercial building were assessed for their work well-being daily for 21 consecutive workdays, while hundreds of chemicals in the office air were continuously measured. Among the well-being metrics assessed, negative emotion was most robustly associated with measures of the net ORP mixture, with an interquartile-range increase corresponding to a 0.054-point increase in negative emotion (95% CI: 0.032–0.076), against a mean score of 1.449 on a 1–5 scale. Associations were also observed for individual ORPs and persisted after adjustment for morning emotional state, copollutants, or other potential confounders in sensitivity analyses. In contrast, ozone, PM2.5, carbon dioxide, and other volatile organic compounds (VOCs) showed weaker or no robust associations. As negative emotion is a sensitive indicator of early mental health risk, the finding underscores broader health implications of ORP exposures that are projected to increase as tropospheric ozone levels increase.</jats:p>

title:
Pesticides
and Tire-Derived
Chemicals in Urban Stormwater
Ponds: Spatiotemporal Dynamics, Co-Occurrence, and Implications for
Environmental Monitoring

affiliation.name: University of Minnesota , , 500 Pillsbury Drive SE , , ,
University of Minnesota , , 500 Pillsbury Drive SE , , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Urban stormwater contains complex mixtures of tire-derived chemicals, pesticides, pharmaceuticals, and other contaminants of emerging concern, yet traditional active monitoring of urban stormwater runoff is severely constrained by precipitation events, high sampling risks, and localized spatial biases. This study evaluates whether stormwater retention ponds serve as passive, spatial–temporal integrators of urban pesticides and tire-derived chemical fingerprints. A regional survey of 13 (sub)urban stormwater retention ponds and year-long, biweekly sampling of a subset of four ponds was combined to characterize the distribution, occurrence, spatial signatures, and temporal dynamics of urban pesticides, tire-derived chemicals, and metformin. Contaminant concentrations in the ponds were similar to those previously observed in stormwater runoff. Distinct temporal dynamics were observed among contaminant classes. Tire-derived chemicals displayed concentration peaks in early spring, whereas peak concentrations of pesticides were detected in early summer. Principal component analysis and Spearman correlations revealed that tire-derived chemicals and urban pesticides co-occurred spatially and temporally. Redundancy analysis and linear mixed-effects models indicated that the spatial distributions of contaminants can be partly explained by land use types within drainage areas. These findings successfully expand the conceptual framework of stormwater retention ponds beyond structural runoff management, establishing them as effective passive spatial–temporal integrators for tracing urban contaminants.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Bottom-up (BU) inventories and top-down (TD) aerial measurements at midstream natural gas facilities frequently diverge, and this discrepancy remains a central challenge for methane accounting in the sector. Previous approaches typically reconcile this divergence by treating BU and TD data as independent estimates of a single true quantity to be adjusted toward agreement, rather than as evidence that each captures only part of a more complex underlying system. This complexity arises from methane emissions being strongly governed by equipment operational state and therefore instantaneous aerial “snapshots” translate poorly to annual inventories. We argue instead that BU and TD are complementary sources of evidence that should be integrated. We present a source-level Bayesian framework that constructs BU prior distributions for each emission source category and updates them with attributed aerial detections through an empirical data-augmentation procedure. The resulting posterior distributions were propagated through unit-level activity data and source-specific information via Monte Carlo simulation to produce annual estimates. Across 64 compressor stations, measurement-integrated annual estimates were 84% higher than the BU inventory, a difference driven almost entirely by compressor vents (rod packing and seal vents) and leakage through blowdown and isolation valves, which together accounted for 90% of the asset-level revision. The revision was heterogeneous across stations and source categories, emphasizing the importance of source-level, station-specific integration when developing an emissions inventory.</jats:p>

title:
Uranium(VI)
Removal from Water by Continuous-Flow
Iron Electrocoagulation: Removal Pathways and Uranium Retention in
Residual Solids
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The removal of uranium(VI) from groundwater is important for both drinking water treatment and pump-and-treat remediation of contaminated aquifers. This study evaluated U(VI) removal by continuous flow-through iron electrocoagulation (EC) under realistic treatment conditions and environmentally relevant water chemistries. The effects of iron dose, pH, dissolved oxygen (DO), dissolved inorganic carbon, and Ca2+ were examined using EC followed by flocculation and sedimentation. Under oxic conditions, U(VI) was removed by adsorption to EC-generated Fe(III) oxides. Under anoxic conditions, U(VI) was removed via a two-step pathway of adsorption followed by reduction to less soluble U(IV) and U(V) species by mixed-valent iron solids (green rust and magnetite). Among the tested combinations of pH (6–8) and DO (oxic and anoxic), the best overall U(VI) removal performance was achieved under oxic pH 7 and anoxic pH 8 conditions. Both conditions gave effective (&gt;90%) removal after 11 s of residence time in the EC reactor, followed by up to 10 min of post-EC treatment with a 10 mg/L Fe dose. Carbonate species and Ca2+ inhibited removal under both oxic and anoxic conditions by forming stable aqueous complexes with U(VI). EC achieved faster and greater U(VI) removal than with chemical coagulation or contact with preformed iron solids. The stability of U removed during anoxic EC was evaluated by exposing residual solids to air. After 24 h of air exposure, only ∼10% of U was released to water. The majority of immobilized U likely remained associated with magnetite. This study provides mechanistic insight into U(VI) removal, solid reactivity, and U stability during EC.</jats:p>

title:
Climate Effect of
Alternative Binders: Life Cycle
Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Potential as a Carbon Sink

affiliation.name: East China University of Political Science and Law , , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Substituting Portland cement (PC) with alternative binders offers a promising pathway to mitigate the climate impacts of the cement industry, one of the most challenging sectors to decarbonize. While substantial greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions are generated during production, most alternative binders can sequester CO2 during their service life. This effect has been acknowledged from a technical perspective, yet its significant influences on the GHG footprint of alternative binders remain unresolved. In this study, we quantify the CO2 uptake of common alternative binders alongside their lifetime GHG emissions. We demonstrate that most binders can take up a larger amount of CO2 than PC during usage, due to a thermodynamically high uptake capacity or high uptake kinetics. The uptake reactions enable a dynamic CO2 loop, with 1–248% of the production emissions being recovered over a 100-year structure service life. However, when the slow reaction rate is considered, the associated climate benefits can be up to 71% lower than the theoretical apparent uptake value. Our results highlight the importance of combined CO2 uptake modeling in assessing the decarbonization potential of alternative binders, and provide a basis for justifying the capability of these binders for use as building carbon sinks.</jats:p>

title:
Human Mitochondrial
HVRII as an Indicator of Island
Groundwater Connectivity
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study explores the use of human mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) as a potential tracer for anthropogenic inputs in confined groundwater systems, building on our previous application in urban watersheds. mtDNA represents one of the most robust sources of eukaryotic environmental DNA (eDNA) due to its multimembrane protection, high copy number per cell, and persistence in the environment, resulting in a valuable resource for both detection and when examining sequences, tracing. We investigated mtDNA transport in the groundwater of Lord Howe Island, a small shield volcano remnant and UNESCO World Heritage site, whose modest population and limited tourist load yield a tractable number of haplotypes. By targeting the hypervariable region II (HVRII) of the human mitochondrial genome, we examined the impact of local human inputs, including septic tanks, on local groundwater. Groundwater samples were collected from wells and small groundwater discharges, PCR-amplified, and analyzed via high-throughput sequencing, revealing unique haplotype frequencies that identified zones of impact. These findings were supported by Bacteroides 16S tracking, using human, bovine, and canine specific markers as well as bacterial counts and other water quality parameters. This approach demonstrates several advantages over more traditional source tracking markers, most importantly, which impacts are uniquely anthropogenic and their origin. Unlike artificial DNA tracers, mtDNA is naturally present in septic tank leach fields and is temporally unambiguous, like plant-based viral markers. Our work highlights mtDNA’s potential to help map anthropogenic inputs within groundwater, which is a tool that may be particularly valuable for island communities with limited wastewater infrastructure resources.</jats:p>

title:
Gas Chromatography-High
Resolution Mass Spectrometry
Spatiotemporal Screening of River Rhine Suspended Particulate Matter
(2005–2022): An Early-Warning Tool for Contaminants of Concern

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Environmental monitoring of archived suspended particulate matter (SPM) provides a basis for retrospective assessment of emerging contaminants in river systems. This study used yearly resolved SPM samples from two sites in the River Rhine, Koblenz and Weil am Rhein, to generate and prioritize gas chromatography high-resolution mass spectrometry (GC-HRMS) data within an early warning system (EWS). The aim was to identify potential contaminants of emerging concern (CEC) showing increasing temporal trends. Of ∼3300 blank-filtered and aligned features, ∼400 exhibited significant trends (p &lt; 0.05), of which ∼80 showed increasing trends. Tentative annotation was performed using spectral libraries which tentatively identified 234 compounds. Cross-referencing tentatively identified compounds showing increasing trends with ECOSAR-modeled aquatic toxicity identified 12 compounds with significant increasing trends and high predicted aquatic toxicity (ρ &gt; 0.6, LC50/EC50 &lt; 1 mg/L). Among the compounds prioritized, tentatively annotated α-methylstyrene oligomers and linear siloxanes accounted for four and three compounds, respectively, indicating recurrent compound-group signals warranting further investigation into their identities, potential co-occurring isomers, concentrations, sources, and subsequently associated risks. Although tentative identification remained a limitation of the GC-HRMS workflow, which relied on hard ionization, these results demonstrate the value of sample archives for temporally resolved prioritization in HRMS-based EWS approaches and highlight their potential for identifying potential CEC.</jats:p>

title:
Oxygen
Vacancies
in Metal-Based Catalysts for Advanced
Oxidation Processes: From Defect States to Reaction Pathways
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Oxygen vacancies (Vo) engineering can regulate oxidant adsorption and interfacial electron transfer in metal-based catalysts for advanced oxidation processes (AOPs), thereby overcoming inefficient oxidant activation, sluggish charge transfer, and limited pathway selectivity. Despite rapid advances in Vo synthesis, characterization, and catalytic applications, a unified understanding of how Vo govern the catalytic process remains lacking. This Review first summarizes the construction, classification, physicochemical properties, and characterization of Vo, followed by a critical evaluation of their identification as catalytically active sites. We then elucidate how Vo regulate the adsorption, activation, and transformation of oxidants and reactants, thereby governing both reactive oxygen species (ROS)-mediated oxidation and electron-transfer processes (ETPs). Particular emphasis is placed on the emerging synergistic interactions between Vo and neighboring active sites, including metal centers, other vacancy defects, and heterojunction interfaces. More importantly, a unified framework is proposed to rationalize the divergent reaction pathways induced by Vo from the perspectives of catalyst–oxidant interactions, Vo concentration, and Vo type. These factors collectively determine local electronic structures, interfacial charge-transfer behaviors, and spin-state evolution, ultimately dictating the pathway selection between ROS generation and ETP. Finally, key challenges in Vo engineering, active-site identification, and pathway discrimination are highlighted together with future opportunities for advancing Vo-mediated AOPs. By shifting the focus from Vo generation to Vo-state regulation, this Review provides guidance for designing next-generation AOP catalysts with tunable reactivity, pathway selectivity, and long-term stability.</jats:p>

title:
Interfacial
Water
Hydrogen-Bond Network Reorientation
Accelerates Advanced Oxidation for Micropollutant Abatement
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Interfacial water rigid hydrogen-bond (HB) networks impose significant thermodynamic and mass-transfer barriers in heterogeneous advanced oxidation processes. Herein, we propose a decoupled interfacial water oxidation process (decoupled interfacial oxidation process (DIOP)) strategy that dynamically reorganizes interfacial water to achieve pronounced kinetic acceleration and high decontamination selectivity. Localized electronic polarization drives cooperative reorientation of interfacial H2O, transforming rigid ice-like water clusters into a dynamic zigzag-like HB configuration. This structural relaxation significantly reduces interfacial solvent reorganization energy, shortens electron tunneling distances, and generates angstrom-scale dynamic low-density water microregions. These fluidic microregions selectively enrich small-molecule pollutants over bulky natural organic matter through dipole alignment and surface binding affinities. Density functional theory calculations and electrochemical analyses demonstrate that interfacial H2O reorientation serves as a pivotal gating step, promoting inner-sphere electron transfer between peracetic acid and target contaminants. The quantum probability density microkinetic model was developed to elucidate the crucial role of interfacial water orientation and HB restructuring frequency in mitigating mass-transfer limitations. Furthermore, the DIOP continuous-flow device achieves a 100% micropollutant removal over 180 h with minimal metal leaching. This work elucidates the role of interfacial H2O dynamics in heterogeneous oxidation, offering a generalizable design strategy for advanced wastewater purification.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Acid treatment of polyamide reverse osmosis (RO) and nanofiltration (NF) membranes is a commonly used approach for membrane cleaning and modification. However, there are contradictory observations on the effects of acid treatment in the current literature. Herein, we systematically characterized the changes in the physicochemical properties of both RO and NF membranes under different acid treatment conditions. Both acid-treated RO and NF membranes exhibited similar surface physicochemical characteristics compared with their respective original membranes. Interestingly, the acid-treated RO membrane showed a nearly doubled water permeance while maintaining high salt rejection. During the acid treatment, the fully aromatic RO membrane underwent selective removal of monomers/oligomers from the bottom region of its asymmetric polyamide layer, as evidenced by the appearance of N-rich molecules in the acid rinsing solution and the increased O/N ratio of the polyamide bottom side. At the same time, the O/N ratio of the polyamide top surface was not affected. In comparison, no release of monomers/oligomers was detected during the acid treatment of the semiaromatic NF membrane. Correspondingly, the NF membrane had a comparable water permeance before and after acid treatment. In the current study, the acid-treated RO membrane demonstrated improved water permeance and stable rejection of NaCl and several micropollutants, suggesting that acid treatment could be used as a polishing strategy to improve the performance of RO membranes for high-efficiency water treatment.</jats:p>

title:
Product
Formation
Dynamics and Sustainability in Chain
Elongation Systems: A Cross-Study Analysis

affiliation.name: The University of New South Wales , , , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>As a promising strategy for sustainable resource recovery under the global energy crisis, chain elongation in anaerobic fermentation systems has attracted increasing attention. However, its optimization is constrained by limited understanding of dynamic behavior and its role in system-level decision-making. Here, we present a data-driven framework that progressively links dynamic process interpretation with predictive modeling and sustainability-oriented evaluation across heterogeneous chain elongation systems. Literature-derived time-series data were first analyzed to characterize product formation kinetics and identify mode-dependent relationships between process evolution and C6 formation. Building on these mechanistic insights, a random forest model using only initial operating conditions was developed to predict key kinetic descriptors, enabling pre-experimental screening of expected process behavior, while a hybrid dynamic model translated kinetic descriptors into complete product formation trajectories. Environmental and economic assessments further revealed substantial trade-offs among cost, product value, and environmental impact, with only 11 of 893 configurations (1.23%) identified as three-objective Pareto-efficient. Overall, this work provides a data-driven basis for identifying process-control priorities, screening operating conditions before extensive experimentation, anticipating product formation dynamics, and selecting configurations against multiple sustainability objectives.</jats:p>

title:
Wildfire-Driven
Release of Endocrine Disrupting Chemicals
from Tree Biomass

affiliation.name: Universidade de Lisboa , , Avenida Rovisco Pais, 1 , ,
Universidade de Lisboa , , Avenida Rovisco Pais, 1 , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Fire-prone regions and longer fire seasons are projected to increase with climate warming, intensifying forest disturbance. Many persistent endocrine disrupting chemicals (EDCs), including polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDEs), per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), can bioaccumulate in forest biomass through long-range atmospheric transport and local deposition, effectively turning forests into contaminant reservoirs. In this Perspective, we expand the concept of wildfire as a driver of remobilization of sequestered EDCs and argue that wildfire can shift forests from sinks to episodic sources of EDC emissions and runoff. We synthesize evidence that EDCs accumulate in tree tissues globally and outline how wildfire may remobilize biomass-sequestered EDCs through coupled atmospheric, terrestrial, and aquatic pathways. Using PFAS as a representative class, we introduce a screening-level model of pre-existing PFAS mass mobilized from burned aboveground wooded biomass. For Greece's 2023 fire season (127,602 ha), a weighted tissue concentration of ∼137.2 ng·g–1 yields a theoretical maximum release of ∼1.22 metric tons (9.6 g·ha–1). Finally, we propose physicochemical criteria to identify EDCs susceptible to wildfire-mediated release and highlight priority research directions to quantify cross-media fluxes in the era of persistent chemical production.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Sulfur mustard (HD) and lewisite (L, mainly containing L1 and L2) from Japanese Abandoned Chemical Weapons (JACWs) in China have persisted for nearly a century, posing ongoing risks to ecological environments and public health. Plants can serve as monitoring sentinels for tracing detection of chemical exposure. However, specific plant biomarkers for HD/L remain unidentified, and their transformation in plants remains unveiled. By nontargeted metabolomics and high-resolution mass spectrometry, 30 novel plant adducts of HD/L were identified. Twelve of these adducts, along with 5 degradation products, were evaluated and assembled into a plant biomarker profile for retrospective detection of HD/L exposure. A sensitive UHPLC–TQ MS method was developed with LODs as low as 0.0200 ng/mL. The profile was detectable in 12 plant species for at least 90 days after exposure. Adduction, hydrolysis, oxidation, and trimerization of HD/L agents have been detected in plants, and transformation diagrams were portrayed. Real samples from JACW remediation sites in northeastern China were analyzed, and free biomarkers were detected at obviously higher levels in plants than in soil. Analytical results indicate that plant leaves may serve as sensitive monitoring media for the exposed agents. This work provides a reliable approach for long-term monitoring of JACW exposure and shows that possible plant accumulation and soil-to-plant transport of CWA products are valuable for further study.</jats:p>

title:
Field Aging of Biochar
Drives SOC Accumulation by
Promoting Photosynthetic Carbon Input and Shifting Soil Microbial
Communities
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Biochar application is an effective strategy for enhancing the soil organic carbon (SOC) sequestration. However, the extent to which biochar aging affects the SOC sequestration remains unclear. In this study, we investigated SOC dynamics, photosynthetic carbon allocation patterns, and soil microbial characteristics across a 1- to 5-year biochar aging gradient in a wheat farmland. The results revealed that the SOC content increased by 20.7% after 1 year of biochar application, primarily because of an increase in particulate organic carbon (POC), and increased by an additional 14.8% over the next 4 years, which resulted from additional increases in both POC and mineral-associated organic carbon (MAOC). The total 13C assimilation increased by 19.9% and 33.0% after 1 and 5 years of biochar application, respectively. Moreover, biochar application promoted the accumulation of 13C in POC, while 5 years of biochar application also increased the assimilated 13C in MAOC. Furthermore, biochar aging altered the soil bacterial community and increased the abundance of saprotrophic fungi, which were strongly related to SOC dynamics. In summary, our results indicate that biochar aging promotes SOC sequestration by promoting photosynthetic carbon assimilation and facilitating the transformation of plant-derived carbon into SOC related to shifts in the soil microbial community.</jats:p>

title:
Meta
Life Cycle Assessment, Techno-Economic Analysis,
and Risk Assessment of Carbon Mineralization Pathways to Inform Policy
Frameworks
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Carbon mineralization can reduce both point-source and legacy CO2 emissions while minimizing long-term risk, and it is essential, urgent, and disconnected. There is no holistic governing carbon mineralization policy in the US or EU, even though carbon capture is already factored into all major global climate models, with mineralization (converting CO2 into stable carbonates) representing a major subset. If mineralization is to bolster the suite of climate mitigation strategies, it is vital that academic guidance be provided to inform the currently underinformed policy direction. To address this, this study presents a meta life cycle and techno-economic analysis of carbon mineralization pathways from both academia and industry, normalizing independent techno-economic, life cycle, and risk assessment (Monte Carlo) results within the context of US and EU policy. Results demonstrate that in situ mineralization achieves the greatest life cycle GHG emission reductions at the lowest cost and is the only pathway capable of gigaton-scale emission reductions commensurate with climate goals. Enhanced rock weathering also consistently delivers net-negative GHG removal at relatively low costs, but ex situ pathways achieve lower GHG emission reductions at higher costs, where several proposed pathways are net-CO2 positive as CO2 emitted throughout the process (transportation, electricity use, and natural gas combustion) offsets CO2 sequestered. Risks of leakage, hazards, global capacity, financial impact, and reversal are also quantitatively and qualitatively compared among the mineralization pathways, demonstrating that in situ mineralization has low financial risk when bolstered by state entities, faces uncertainties in non-governmental organization objection, and, ultimately, all pathways are victims of uncharted policy.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Sewer sediments contain dense biofilms enriched with extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), which severely impede chemical infiltration and hinder sediment control. This study uses micro-nano bubbles (MNBs) for the first time to remodel the three-dimensional structure of sewer sediments and reduce their EPS content, thereby enhancing their permeability. Three-dimensional structural analysis revealed that sewer sediments consist of cluster (0.78 mm) and bridged (0.12 mm) biofilms, forming a dense gel network with low porosity. When 20% MNBs were introduced, the complete tracer penetration time decreased from 36 to 8 h, representing a 3.5-times faster migration speed than the baseline group. X-ray computed tomography revealed that MNBs disrupted the sediment matrix: tortuosity decreased from 1.754 to 1.352, the pore volume fraction increased from 0.083 to 0.105, and the number of cluster biofilms decreased from 280 to 178. EPS analysis indicated substantial depth-dependent reductions in protein (5.6 to 1.4 mg/g VSS) and polysaccharide (3.8 to 1.9 mg/g VSS) contents. Finally, the oxidation–reduction potential increased from −280 to −88 mV, shifting the dominant microbial community from anaerobic to aerobic. The underlying mechanism involved the synergistic effects of structural remodeling and EPS reduction, providing theoretical support for applying MNB technology to urban sewage pipe maintenance.</jats:p>

title:
Source
Attribution, Driving Force Interpretation,
and Nature-Based Mitigation of Anthropogenic Water Pollution

affiliation.name: Sino-Danish Centre for Education and Research , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Anthropogenic pollution induced by combined sewer overflow (CSO) threatens urban aquatic ecosystems, yet the source contributions and driving mechanisms of its pollutants from surface runoff and domestic wastewater remain unclear. Here, we propose an analytical framework coupling high-resolution water quality modeling with climatic and socioeconomic (SSP-RCP) projections to characterize spatiotemporal dynamics and source contributions of CSO pollution under changing environments. Random Forest (RF) with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was employed to identify critical drivers of each source. Lorenz curves and Gini coefficient were introduced to evaluate nature-based solutions (NbS) against extreme CSOs. Application of the framework in a typical urban area demonstrated the dominant contribution of runoff pollution (78–88%) to annual loads of 2500–4200 tons, with uncertainty bounds (UB) of 2300–5800 tons. RF-SHAP analysis revealed nonlinear pollution exacerbation around transition points of approximately 8 days for dry-weather period, 0.45 for surface imperviousness, and 2000 inhabitants/km2 for population density. NbS practices mitigated 19–77% of runoff pollution and 52–76% of domestic pollution, decreasing Gini coefficients from 0.69 to 0.49 (UB: 0.40–0.82). The findings provide quantitative support for compliance with the EU Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive, offering a replicable reference for pollution attribution, driver identification, and mitigation assessment under changing environments.</jats:p>

title:
Shrinking Non-CO2 Emission Inequality in
China’s Municipal Wastewater Treatment
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Integrating emission equity into climate mitigation is essential for sustainable development but remains poorly understood in the wastewater-treatment sector. Here, we develop a long-term, high-resolution emission inventory covering 8703 municipal wastewater treatment plants across China from 2001 to 2020 to assess methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O) emission trends and their spatial inequality. National emissions increased substantially, although growth rates slowed after 2010 for CH4 and 2015 for N2O. Discrepancies with IPCC-derived estimates highlight the limitations of population-based approaches in capturing emission trends. Economic development dominated emission growth, with wastewater treatment intensity (wastewater treated per unit of GDP) contributing positively, even under scenarios that account for potential changes in emission factors associated with technological and management improvements. Significant emission inequality persisted, with economically developed cities (9% of the population) contributing 16% and 15% of CH4 and N2O emissions in 2020, whereas the least developed group (45% of the population) accounted for 28% and 32%, respectively. Nonetheless, this disparity narrowed over time with Gini coefficients falling from 0.54 to 0.26 for CH4 and from 0.51 to 0.22 for N2O. These findings support geographically differentiated mitigation strategies that prioritize high-emitting areas to promote effective and equitable climate mitigation.</jats:p>

title:
Depth-Dependent
eDNA Abundances across Ecosystems
Inform Deep-Sea Sampling Strategies

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Environmental DNA (eDNA) surveys are increasingly used to assess marine biodiversity and inform deep-sea environmental decision-making, including mineral resource management and fisheries oversight. Yet standard low-volume protocols inherited from coastal work may be inadequate at depth, and recent findings indicate that depth- and productivity-aware sampling, often requiring high-volume in situ filtration, is needed. Currently no quantitative framework links depth and ecosystem context to define defensible filtration volume targets. We compiled 841 eDNA samples from eight expeditions across the North Atlantic, Wider Caribbean Region, and Pacific (surface to 4000 m) to quantify how recoverable eDNA scales with depth and surface productivity, and to derive depth- and productivity-aware sampling targets. Total eDNA concentration declined with depth as a power law, with attenuation exponents (b) modulated by surface productivity: most gradual in eutrophic waters (b = 0.67), intermediate in mesotrophic (b = 0.90), and steepest in oligotrophic systems (b = 1.25). Volume-weighted models explained 66–88% of the variance. At a fixed extract-concentration target, required filtration volumes diverged ∼7-fold between oligotrophic and eutrophic systems at 200 m and ∼38-fold at 4000 m. Conventional Niskin sampling therefore undersamples deep-sea animal eDNA, particularly in mid- to low-productivity systems. Among laboratory parameters, the assay-specific extract-concentration target exerted greater leverage on required volume than extraction efficiency or elution volume. Volume-aware sampling paired with optimized recovery should be routine in deep-sea eDNA surveys.</jats:p>

title:
Drivers of Regional
Aerosol pH Differences over Eastern
China Quantified with a Thermodynamic Framework

affiliation.name: Hebei University of Science and Technology , , ,

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Aerosol pH governs atmospheric multiphase chemistry, yet quantifying its regional drivers consistently across meteorologically and chemically diverse regions within a single thermodynamically accurate framework remains challenging. Here, we couple the regional chemical transport model Weather Research and Forecasting-Goddard Earth Observing System with Chemistry (WRF-GC) with the Extended Aerosol Inorganics Model (E-AIM) to compute wintertime aerosol pH over six key target regions of eastern China, decompose the drivers of regional pH differences and intramonthly variability through an ammonia gas-particle partitioning framework, and extend this framework to a scenario-response analysis. Monthly mean pH ranges from 2.54 to 4.32, more acidic in the south and more alkaline at higher latitudes. Temperature is the leading driver of the regional pH deviation in the YRD, PRD, and NEP (contributing 58%–63%), whereas in the high-emission NCP and FWP the deviation is instead dominated by NH3 (41%–58%). Negative covariance among the drivers substantially damps intramonthly pH fluctuations, consistent with multiphase buffering. The sensitivity of pH to ammonia reduction rises sharply as aerosols approach an ammonia-poor regime, such that large emission reductions of ammonia would decrease wintertime aerosol pH well beyond linear expectations, with pronounced inter-regional differences. By resolving these drivers on benchmark-level thermodynamics, these results provide a quantitative, region-specific basis for anticipating how aerosol pH responds to differentiated emission-reduction strategies.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Environmental contamination from an ever-increasing number of chemicals is a subject of high concern, with over one hundred thousand discrete chemicals listed in a recently compiled open global chemical inventory (GCI). As these compounds enter the environment, they often form transformation products (TPs) which may have persistent, mobile, and toxic (PMT) properties. Despite this, less than 1% of compounds have openly available TP information. Although TP prediction can fill some data gaps, the models are prone to combinatorial explosion, and predicted TPs must be prioritized. This study implemented multistep environmental biotic and novel abiotic TP prediction of the ZeroPM GCI chemicals using BioTransformer 4.0, combined with toxicity and mobility models to prioritize which TPs are potentially persistent, mobile, and toxic. The resulting GCI-TPs database contains over 13 million predicted TPs, including 5481 compounds labeled as potential dead-end compounds (compounds that are not predicted to transform further), of which 478 were predicted to be either PMT or PvM compounds. From this, 38 substructures that can act as flags for potential PMT-TP formation were identified. The dead-end PMT-TPs are available on the NORMAN Suspect List Exchange and through the GCI-TPs website (https://gcitps.lcsb.uni.lu/).</jats:p>

title: Dual Pathways of Fe2+ Uptake Drive Intracellular Fenton Chemistry and Ferroptosis-like Cell Death of Escherichia coli upon Exposure to Reduced Nontronite
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Reduced iron-containing clay (RIC) minerals display strong antibacterial activity, yet the intracellular processes underlying bacterial cell death remain poorly understood. Herein, Escherichia coli knockout strains were exposed to a model RIC mineral, reduced nontronite (rNAu-2), to dissect iron influx pathways and the resulting oxidative damage. Two complementary mechanisms of Fe2+ influx were identified: (i) active transport through FeoB proteins and (ii) passive permeation across oxidatively compromised membranes. At low rNAu-2 loading, a feoB mutant accumulated less labile Fe and survived better than the E. coli wild-type (WT), whereas at higher loading, passive permeation dominated and the genotypic differences diminished. Intracellular radical analysis revealed hydroxyl radicals (•OH) as the predominant cytotoxic species. Deleting superoxide dismutases (sodA or sodC) improved bacterial survival by limiting H2O2 availability, whereas loss of peroxidase (ahpC) or catalase (katG) activity elevated H2O2 and •OH production, and heightened cellular vulnerability. rNAu-2 exposure promoted lipid peroxidation and malondialdehyde accumulation, while increasing reliance on glutathione biosynthesis (gshA), indicative of ferroptosis-like cell death. Correspondingly, a recombination-deficient mutant (recA) was hypersensitive to rNAu-2, underscoring the role of oxidative DNA damage in bacterial cell death. These results elucidate the molecular mechanisms of RIC-mediated bacterial killing and significantly advance the current model of antibacterial clay activity.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Hydroxymethanesulfonate (HMS) is a substantial contributor to atmospheric particulate sulfur, yet its accurate quantification remains challenging due to chemical instability, poor chromatographic separation from sulfate, and the lack of a robust routine filter method. Here, we developed a hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)-based differential ion chromatography method that overcomes these limitations. Under optimized conditions (n(H2O2):n(HMS) ≥ 4:1, 60 °C, 30 min), HMS conversion to sulfate reaches 97.5 ± 0.3%, enabling indirect quantification via the stable sulfate signal. Recovery on spiked filters was 99.6 ± 1.4% across 0.025–10 mg L–1, with a method detection limit of 0.018 mg L–1. Application to ∼180 PM2.5 samples from a rural North China Plain site shows HMS is not confined to winter haze: autumn concentrations (mean 0.59 ± 0.70 μg m–3, maximum 3.75 μg m–3) were comparable to or higher than winter values, associated with high relative humidity and elevated formaldehyde. Archived filters lost ∼25% of HMS within one month, suggesting historical data may be biased low. The relative contribution of HMS to particulate sulfur increases as total sulfur loading decreases, implying SO2 emission reductions alone may not diminish HMS chemistry. This method provides a robust framework for accurate HMS measurement and improved sulfur budget closure.</jats:p>

title:
Tire-Derived
Chemicals in Human Populations: A Global

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Tire wear generates diverse tire-derived chemicals (TDCs), including antioxidants, accelerators, and their transformation products, yet human internal exposure remains poorly characterized. This review provides the first systematic synthesis of global biomonitoring evidence for TDCs in human populations, integrating exposure pathways, biological barrier penetration, and preliminary epidemiological findings. Biomonitoring data spanning four continents reveal widespread detection of multiple TDC classes such as p-phenylenediamines (PPDs), p-phenylenediamine quinones (PPD-Qs), benzothiazoles (BTHs), and benzotriazoles (BTRs), in urine and blood, with urinary concentrations consistently exceeding blood levels. Compound-specific patterns, including the predominance of 6PPD-Q over its parent compound 6PPD and substantial contributions from additional congeners (e.g., DPPD-Q, IPPD-Q, 1-OH-BTR), indicate that single-compound biomarkers are insufficient for capturing overall TDC exposure. TDCs have been detected in cord blood, amniotic fluid, cerebrospinal fluid, breast milk, and semen, documenting occurrence across multiple biological compartments and potential exposure during critical developmental windows. Preliminary epidemiological associations link TDC exposure to adverse birth outcomes, neurodevelopmental effects, and carcinogenic risks, though evidence remains constrained by limited sample sizes and narrow geographic representation: China-based studies dominate the literature, while regions with extensive environmental TDC monitoring (e.g., Europe, North America) largely lack corresponding human data, a mismatch that hinders exposure pathway attribution. Collectively, these findings indicate that TDCs represent a ubiquitous but underrecognized human exposure, and we outline priority considerations for risk assessment, including vulnerable population protection, congener-specific mixture effects, analytical standardization, and interim biomonitoring reference values.</jats:p>

title:
Quantifying the
Vehicle Emission Reduction Required
to Offset Warming-Driven Ozone Increase in Beijing
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Vehicle emissions (VE) reductions are a key pathway for mitigating urban ozone pollution, but their effectiveness under the condition of warming-driven biogenic emission responses remains unclear. An ozone formation path tracing (OFPT) method coupling an observation-based model (OBM) with Positive Matrix Factorization (PMF) was used to quantify the contribution of different VOCs for different emission sources to the ozone production rate (PO3). In this study, initial VOC concentrations were reconstructed by correcting for photochemical losses, and an additional constraint on isoprene was applied to improve the assessment of ozone production in Beijing. The results show that initial VOC reconstruction substantially increased PO3 and changed source attribution. Biogenic emissions became the largest single contributor to PO3, whereas VE remained the dominant controllable anthropogenic source because it supplied both VOCs and NOx. After considering the temperature response of isoprene emissions, a 10.7 ± 3.5% reduction in VE was required to offset the O3 increase caused by a 1 °C temperature rise under current conditions. Future-scenario simulations showed that the required VE reductions were lower under the Clean Air scenario (7.1 ± 0.7%) than under the Baseline scenario (11.3 ± 0.1%). These results highlight the need to integrate vehicle electrification, biogenic VOC responses, and warming effects into future ozone control strategies.</jats:p>

title: Distinct Phyllosphere Microbiome-Linked Stress Pathways of Conventional and Biodegradable Plastics in Vallisneria natans

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Microplastics negatively affect submerged macrophytes, but the phyllosphere pathways associated with these responses remain poorly understood, particularly for biodegradable microplastics. Using a mesocosm experiment that distinguished fresh and withered leaf microhabitats, the stress pathways induced by conventional polystyrene (PS) and biodegradable polylactide acid (PLA) in Vallisneria natans were directly compared. Withered leaves emerged as the key microhabitat where the two polymers differed most clearly. PS was mainly associated with host-centered physiological adjustment and a modular microbial network, whereas PLA was associated with broader phyllosphere reorganization, particularly in fresh-leaf bacteria and withered-leaf algal assemblages. Direct measurements in the highest-exposure treatments detected PLA hydrolysis products (lactic acid and oligomers) and PS oxidation products, providing chemical evidence consistent with these contrasting pathways. Mantel tests and structural equation modeling further supported a divergence between a predominantly host-centered PS pathway and a broader PLA pathway involving nutrient balance and phyllosphere organization. These results indicate that conventional and biodegradable microplastics may differ not only in their direct interactions with submerged macrophytes but also in the extent to which microbiome-linked indirect pathways are involved.</jats:p>

title:
Proton-Coupled
Oxidation
Mechanisms in the Ferrate
System: Unraveling the pH Dependence of Fe(VI), Fe(V), and Fe(IV)
for Contaminant Abatement
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Like conventional water treatment oxidants, ferrate exhibits highly pH-dependent reaction kinetics, classically attributed to its acid–base speciation. However, while this dissociation equilibrium accurately describes the kinetics of ferrate decay, it cannot account for the anomalous pH-dependent kinetics observed during contaminant oxidation. By combining acid–base model with the pyrophosphate sequestering method, we reveal that highly reactive Fe(V) and Fe(IV) intermediates drive this deviation. To trace these species, aniline, theophylline, and sulfamethoxazole were employed as model contaminants for oxidation processes dominated by Fe(VI), Fe(V), and Fe(IV), respectively. By quantifying their specific contributions, we found that decreasing pH enhances the reactivity of the intermediates and amplifies their oxidation contributions by 13–63%. Consequently, the systems dominated by Fe(V) or Fe(IV) exhibit apparent rate constants surging far beyond the predictive capacity of the Fe(VI) speciation. Solvent kinetic isotope effects and proton inventory analyses elucidated distinct proton-assisted pathways: Fe(VI) undergoes a rapid protonation pre-equilibrium before rate-limiting electron transfer, Fe(V) reacts via a concerted proton–electron transfer pathway, and Fe(IV) proceeds through an inner-sphere electron transfer pathway associated with coordinated water release. Exploiting these insights, we demonstrate a proton-activation strategy where rapid proton exchange significantly enhances both reaction kinetics and oxidant utilization efficiency in ferrate-based water treatment.</jats:p>

title: Mechanochemistry-Induced Hydrated Salt Activation for Green Recovery of Palladium and Platinum via O 2 -Mediated Oxidation
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Palladium (Pd) and platinum (Pt) are essential precious metals in modern catalytic applications, while their sustainable recovery remains a significant challenge. Herein, we report a room-temperature, AlCl3·6H2O-assisted mechanochemical strategy for efficient recovery of Pd and Pt from industrial spent catalysts and automotive three-way catalysts without the addition of external oxidants. Mechanistic investigations reveal that mechanochemical treatment promotes catalyst fragmentation and the activation of hydrated salt, creating an ion-rich, liquid-like interfacial environment that facilitates O2-mediated oxidation of metallic Pd and Pt and stabilizes the oxidized metal species through chloride coordination. High-purity Pd and Pt products were successfully recovered through water extraction and N2H4·H2O reduction, while the recyclable AlCl3·6H2O medium enabled a closed-loop process with reduced reagent consumption. A preliminary lab-scale cost assessment indicated treatment costs comparable to those of conventional aqua regia treatment, highlighting the potential of hydrated salt-assisted mechanochemistry as a mild, recyclable, and economically promising approach for sustainable Pd and Pt recovery.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Dissolved organic matter (DOM) plays important roles in numerous processes in both natural and engineered systems, ranging from carbon cycling to metal complexation to disinfection byproduct formation. Characterizing the composition of this complex mixture, which is comprised of thousands of molecules that vary in time and space, is critical for understanding its role and reactivity. This review highlights major developments and notable limitations in the most commonly used DOM analytical techniques and, importantly, summarizes state-of-the-art knowledge on DOM composition and reactivity gained from each approach. The selected techniques include simple but fundamental approaches for DOM analysis (i.e., chromatography and optical spectroscopy), more complex molecular techniques (i.e., nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy and ultrahigh- and high-resolution mass spectrometry), and methods designed to investigate reactivity (i.e., electrochemical analyses). The review also assesses prospects and needs for future developments within each technique, which range from further advancing analytical capabilities to making instrumentation more accessible to improved data analysis. Finally, because each technique is only able to partially describe DOM composition and reactivity, the review provides a forward-looking outlook on combined analytical approaches and opportunities for data synthesis, leveraging the potential of complementary analytical techniques to establish a more integrated understanding of DOM composition and reactivity.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are widely used in functional textiles for water- and stain resistance, yet their polymer compositions, quantities, and potential environmental release remain poorly resolved by conventional analyses. Here, we analyzed 22 commercial textiles using an integrated approach combining total fluorine (TF) by combustion ion chromatography, targeted PFAS analysis, the total oxidizable precursor (TOP) assay, and pyrolysis–gas chromatography–high-resolution mass spectrometry (Py-GC-HRMS); the latter enabled polymer-specific identification and semiquantitative estimation of fluoropolymer and side-chain fluorinated polymer (SCFP) contributions. Fifteen textiles contained low-to-moderate TF concentrations (0.03–2.57 mg F g–1) and were predominantly associated with SCFPs containing 6:2 and/or 8:2 fluorotelomer moieties, whereas three high-fluorine textiles (143–158 mg F g–1) contained polytetrafluoroethylene together with SCFP-based treatments. Targeted PFAS accounted for ≤0.021% of TF, while TOP-derived PFAS also represented only a small additional fraction, indicating that conventional extractable and oxidizable PFAS measurements captured little of the total fluorine inventory. Simulated laundering, UV exposure, and wet abrasion caused limited TF loss in most textiles but substantial losses in some SCFP-treated materials, indicating treatment-dependent potential for PFAS-associated fluorine release during use and aging. This approach improves polymer-specific characterization of PFAS in textiles and helps assess their potential environmental emissions.</jats:p>

title:

Geogenic Contaminants Induced by Seawater
Intrusion in Coastal Aquifers Globally

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Seawater intrusion deteriorates freshwater quality in coastal aquifers, threatening billions of people worldwide. While its impacts on freshwater scarcity and salinization are well documented, the associated mobilization of geogenic contaminants remains unclear. This study critically reviews the current knowledge on the global distribution, underlying biogeochemical mechanisms, specific triggering scenarios, management implications, and predictive modeling advances of seawater-intrusion-induced contaminant mobilization. A synthesis of 343 studies across 55 countries confirms the widespread occurrence of geogenic contamination in coastal aquifers. Among these, studies from 19 countries (n = 50) document seawater-intrusion-related contaminant mobilization. At the microscale, contaminant release is driven by altered water–rock interactions, disrupted microbial metabolism, and colloidal transport. These biogeochemical shifts are further modulated by specific seawater intrusion scenarios such as groundwater overexploitation, sea-level rise, and tidal oscillation. Of particular concern, conventional strategies for mitigating seawater intrusion may inadvertently alter aquifer hydrochemistry and intensify contaminant release, underscoring the urgent need for optimized synergistic solutions. While some reactive transport models attempt to capture these dynamics, their field-scale accuracy remains constrained by hydrogeological heterogeneities and computational bottlenecks. Addressing these challenges requires multidisciplinary collaboration and high-resolution monitoring of databases. These advances are critical to informing science-driven governance frameworks that ensure the long-term sustainability of coastal groundwater resources.</jats:p>

title: Physiological Adaptation of Comammox Nitrospira to Acidic pH Suppresses N2O Production

affiliation.name: Shenzhen Campus of Sun Yat-Sen University , , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Nitrous oxide (N2O), a potent greenhouse gas, is a major byproduct of microbial nitrification, yet how environmental pH governs N2O production by complete ammonia oxidizers (comammox) remains poorly understood. We conducted controlled culture experiments with comammox Nitrospira inopinata at pH 6.5, 7.5, and 8.5. Under mild acidification (pH 6.5), nitrification activity was largely maintained, but cellular growth declined sharply, and both N2O yield and extracellular hydroxylamine (NH2OH) accumulation fell substantially relative to neutral conditions. Strikingly, this reduced growth was accompanied by pronounced transcriptional upregulation of core nitrification, stress response, and pH homeostasis genes, whereas carbon fixation genes remained largely unchanged. This decoupling of growth from gene expression indicates that acid-stressed cells reallocate energy away from biosynthesis toward cellular maintenance and proton extrusion, tightening intracellular handling of NH2OH and limiting its extracellular release. Isotopomer analysis (site preference ∼28–36‰) confirmed that NH2OH-driven chemistry remained the dominant N2O source across all pH conditions, and complementary abiotic assays indicated that chemical N2O formation was likely influenced by the diminished NH2OH pool. These results establish that comammox suppresses, rather than enhances, N2O production under mild acidification, opposite to the response reported for canonical ammonia-oxidizing microbes. This distinctive trait carries important implications for predicting nitrification-derived N2O fluxes and refining greenhouse-gas budgets in acidifying ecosystems.</jats:p>

title:
Decoding and Harnessing
Microbial Resilience for Anaerobic
Digestion: Mechanisms, Strategies, and Sustainability under Environmental
Stress
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Anaerobic digestion (AD) is central to the circular bioeconomy, yet its application is limited by the vulnerability of microbial consortia to diverse stressors from endogenous metabolic inhibitors to exogenous contaminants. This Review synthesizes current evidence on microbial resilience mechanisms in AD, distinguishing resistance from perturbation to functional recovery through a sensing-activation-adaptation cascade. The thermodynamic basis of stability is examined through discoveries in direct interspecies electron transfer (DIET) and metabolic bifurcation, revealing how syntrophic networks overcome thermodynamic barriers under stress. Multiscale resilience mechanisms are considered from molecular sensors and signal transduction pathways to community-level reorganization associated with functional redundancy and niche differentiation. Bridging microbial ecology with process engineering, resilience-enhancing strategies are evaluated, including quorum sensing manipulation, conductive material amendment, and bioaugmentation with immobilized consortia, strengthening syntrophic networks under internal and external perturbations. A shift from reactive monitoring to proactive management is discussed, using interpretable deep learning models and genome-informed digital twins to predict failures. Critical knowledge gaps include single-cell phenotypic heterogeneity and the synthetic consortium design. Resilient AD systems require a framework integrating techno-economic viability with life cycle assessment, ensuring that they are biologically robust, environmentally sustainable, and economically competitive under variable operating conditions.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ozone pollution control is mainly based on the ozone chemistry sensitivity to precursor emissions. However, despite stringent reductions in precursor emissions, severe summer ozone pollution persistently engulfs the North China Plain (NCP), urgently calling for effective ozone controls. Here, we show that there is strong interfacial ozone exchange between free troposphere (FT) and atmospheric boundary layer (ABL), which renders FT ozone a potential source of surface ozone, but has not been well accounted for in previous ozone controls. We quantify FT-ABL interfacial ozone exchange using an online diagnostic scheme implemented in a coupled meteorology-chemistry model and reveal a significant yet spatially heterogeneous correlation between observed surface ozone and interfacial exchange over the NCP. In high-correlation area, strong downward transport from FT to ABL exceeds chemical production, contributing 52% of afternoon ozone sources under polluted conditions. In low-correlation area, ozone pollution is dominated by chemical production. Derived from these spatially differentiated pollution causes, we propose an expanded ozone pollution formation regime to divide the NCP into exchange-dominated, chemistry-dominated, and mixed conditions. This new regime can better explain observed and modeled spatial differences of ozone trends in response to precursor reductions in 2019–2025. Our results highlight the importance of incorporating FT-ABL interfacial exchange into ozone pollution control frameworks beyond conventional chemistry-based regime.</jats:p>

Quantile g-computation indicated that a simultaneous one-quartile increase in the Co–Cu–Sr mixture was associated with 48.07 g higher birth weight (95% CI: 7.13–89.02 g). title: Physiological and Transcriptomic Responses of Thalassiosira pseudonana to Coated ZnO Nanoparticles and Their Mixtures under Long-Term, Low-Dose Exposure: The Dominant Role of Dissolved Zinc

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The escalating production of engineered nanomaterials has raised concerns about their environmental impact. However, conventional short-term, high-dose ecotoxicity studies inadequately reflect realistic exposure scenarios. This study evaluated the long-term, low-dose toxicity of bare zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO-NPs) and four representative silane-modified ZnO-NPs in the marine diatom Thalassiosira pseudonana. Algal cells were exposed for 14 days to individual ZnO-NPs, their binary mixtures (0.001–1 mg/L) or equimolar Zn2+ (0.0008–0.8 mg/L). Physiological and transcriptomic responses showed dose- and time-dependent toxicity, with largely comparable effects across nanoparticle and Zn2+ treatments. Growth inhibition by all zinc forms peaked at 38.0% within 0.01–0.1 mg/L and exceeded 90.0% at 1 mg/L, accompanied by reduced photosynthetic performance, altered chlorophyll a content, and elevated lipid peroxidation. Transcriptomic profiles of all ZnO-NPs resembled those of Zn2+, particularly for photosynthesis- and oxidative stress-related pathways. These similar responses were likely attributable to the substantial dissolution of all nanoparticles and their mixtures (44.3–89.2%), resulting in comparable cellular zinc bioaccumulation and Zn2+-like toxicity. Together, these findings reflect that the tested ZnO-NPs, whether silane-modified or present in mixtures, may behave similarly to dissolved zinc under chronic, environmentally relevant concentrations, highlighting the importance of incorporating such scenarios into ecological risk assessments of soluble metal-based nanomaterials.</jats:p>

title:
Quantifying the
Contribution of Primary, Secondary,
and Tertiary Amines to Nitrogenous Disinfection Byproduct Formation
in Wastewater by Chemical Derivatization
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Disinfection of wastewater effluent during water reuse produces nitrogenous disinfection byproducts (N-DBPs), many of which are more toxic than regulated DBPs. Despite progress in understanding N-DBP formation pathways from model compounds, the precursors of N-DBPs in authentic wastewater effluent remain largely unknown. Using derivatization reactions adapted from the synthetic organic chemistry literature, this study quantified the contribution of 1°, 2°, and 3° amines to the formation of three commonly studied N-DBP classes in wastewater effluent: N-nitrosamines, nitroalkanes, and haloacetonitriles. Derivatization reactions were first adapted to mild reaction conditions, and then derivatization effectiveness at suppressing N-DBP formation was assessed with known N-DBP precursors. Effluent organic matter was similarly derivatized to selectively block 1°, 1° and 2°, or all amines, and N-DBP formation after disinfection was compared to nonderivatized controls. NDMA formation was primarily attributable to secondary amines; nitromethane formation was attributable to primary amines, with secondary amines sometimes contributing significantly; and haloacetonitrile precursors varied by source, chiefly primary amines in two wastewaters, but secondary amines in another. Irrespective of amine order (1°/2°/3°), amines collectively comprised the majority of the N-DBP precursor pool, suggesting that insights from N-DBP formation mechanism studies using amines as model precursors are likely applicable to real wastewater.</jats:p>
